title: The Last Winter
premise: When his identical twin brother Ezra dies under murky circumstances, Gideon Crane returns to the family homestead in rural Vermont to bury him — only to discover Ezra's journals describing a door unearthed by the excavation crew on the old Crane land, sealed from the inside, and a debt the family has owed since 1974. As Gideon documents the escalating wrongness around the house, he learns Ezra didn't die: he was taken as payment, and the thing behind the door has mistaken Gideon for him, twin for twin, debt for debt. To save himself and end the Crane curse, Gideon must return what their grandfather stole in 1974 — the bones of the family's first-born, buried beneath the foundation — even if it means giving the door something of himself in trade. In the end, Gideon seals the door from the inside in his brother's place, and his own documentation becomes the record that lets the last Crane rest.
about_author: Petra Crane is the pseudonym of a former county archivist who spent a decade cataloguing estate records in northern New England, where she developed a deep unease about what families choose to write down. She writes horror about inheritance, paperwork, and the things that wait patiently for their names to be spoken.

chapters.title: Inventory of the Dead
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. He arrives at the Crane homestead with a body bag and a filing case, cataloguing Ezra's belongings with ritual precision. The house smells of turned earth though nothing has been dug. Emotional beat: grief expressed as bureaucracy, and the first crack in it — Ezra's journal, last entry unfinished, dated the day he died.

chapters.title: The Wrong Twin
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Neighbors at the wake keep calling him Ezra, and one old woman, Marge Voss, grips his wrist and says, 'You came back. It said you would.' Gideon assumes senility. Emotional beat: the uncanny comfort of being mistaken for someone loved, curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Ezra's Ledger
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, interleaved with Ezra's journal entries. The journals describe the excavation crew's discovery: a door of black oak set into bedrock, sealed from the inside, warm to the touch. The final entry breaks off mid-sentence. Emotional beat: Gideon realizes his brother was documenting too — documentation as prayer, inherited like the house.

chapters.title: What the Crew Found
chapters.summary: Gideon interviews Dale Hutchins, the excavation foreman, who is drinking heavily and won't go back on the property. He describes the door, the heat, and how the crew's youngest man walked into the tree line and never came out. Emotional beat: denial collapsing; Gideon starts a new notebook labeled 'EVIDENCE.'

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Four
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. In the county archive he finds the deed history and a sealed court file: in 1974 their grandfather Silas Crane was charged, then quietly released, in the disappearance of a child. The excavation site sits exactly where the old foundation was. Emotional beat: the family name he inherited is a debt instrument.

chapters.title: The Warm Door
chapters.summary: Gideon descends into the excavation at night. The door is exactly as Ezra described, and when he presses his palm to it, it presses back. Scratching sounds — rhythmic, patient — from the other side. Emotional beat: terror and a terrible recognition, like hearing his own heartbeat from inside a wall.

chapters.title: Marge Voss Remembers
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Marge tells him about 1974: the missing child was the Voss girl, and Silas didn't take her — he bought something with her, a bargain to save his dying wife. 'Your family paid once,' she says. 'The door keeps a ledger too.' Emotional beat: inheritance reframed as complicity.

chapters.title: Twin Static
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. He begins dreaming Ezra's dreams: the other side of the door, a hallway of Crane family portraits with the faces scratched out. He wakes with dirt under his fingernails. The door has started mistaking him for Ezra. Emotional beat: identity eroding at the edges; he documents his own hands each morning to prove they're his.

chapters.title: The Second Body
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Dale Hutchins is found dead in his truck at the property line, doors locked from inside, face frozen in a scream despite the mild night. In his pocket: a note in Dale's handwriting reading 'IT'S NOT EZRA. IT'S WORSE. IT'S PATIENT.' Emotional beat: the stakes widen; witnesses are being closed like accounts.

chapters.title: Silas's Confession
chapters.summary: Gideon finds a hidden compartment in the grandfather clock — Silas's confession, 1974. He didn't kill the Voss girl; he traded her bones to the door in exchange for his wife's life, and buried the truth beneath the new foundation. 'What was taken must be returned,' it ends, 'or the door will collect in twins.' Emotional beat: the full weight of the inheritance lands.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Beneath the collapsed foundation stones he uncovers a small tin box: child-sized bones, wrapped in a christening gown, and a Voss family locket. The moment he touches them, every light in the house goes warm and amber, like something exhaling. Emotional beat: grief for a stranger, and the first sense that restitution is possible.

chapters.title: The Door Opens Inward
chapters.summary: Gideon carries the box to the excavation. The door is open — a hand's width — and Ezra's voice comes through, perfectly preserved, asking Gideon to help him out. It knows things only Ezra knew. Emotional beat: the cruelest temptation; loyalty weaponized against truth.

chapters.title: Marge's Warning
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Marge reveals she was there in 1974, that the door speaks in the voices of whoever you're trying to save, and that her sister went in listening to their mother's voice. 'It doesn't want the bones,' she says. 'It wants a Crane on the other side of the ledger.' Emotional beat: Marge's guilt meeting Gideon's resolve.

chapters.title: The House Keeps Records
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The journals, Silas's confession, the county files — Gideon assembles the complete account and reads it aloud in the kitchen, a formal record of the debt. The house responds: doors open, walls sweat, the temperature climbs toward body heat. Emotional beat: documentation as exorcism; naming the crime strips the door of its ambiguity.

chapters.title: Ezra, or the Thing That Was Ezra
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The voice at the door stops pretending. It speaks in Gideon's own voice now, offering a bargain: the bones returned, the debt closed, and Ezra released — if Gideon signs himself over as collateral, twin for twin, forever. Emotional beat: the central choice crystallizes; loyalty vs. truth made literal.

chapters.title: The Voss Locket
chapters.summary: Gideon returns the locket to Marge, who finally weeps. She gives him her sister's true name — Abigail Voss — the name Silas never recorded, the omission that kept the debt open. 'Names are the currency,' Marge says. 'You have to give it back its name.' Emotional beat: truth as the only real payment.

chapters.title: Winter Comes Early
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Frost in July. The property's boundaries contract nightly; the tree line moves closer to the house. Ezra's body in the funeral home is found desiccated, as though something has been drawing him down to nothing, and with him, Gideon's reflection grows fainter. Emotional beat: time running out made physical.

chapters.title: The Return
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. At the door, he reads the full record aloud — Silas's crime, Abigail's name, the family's complicity — and passes the tin box through the gap. The scratching stops. The warmth drains. For one long moment, silence, and then Ezra's actual voice, small and far: 'Gideon? It let me go.' Emotional beat: restitution working — and the trap snapping shut, because the ledger still needs a Crane.

chapters.title: Twin for Twin
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Ezra crawls out, half-alive, and the door begins to close with Gideon on the wrong side of the threshold. The twins grapple at the frame — the thing inside wearing both their faces now. Emotional beat: the climax; loyalty means Ezra trying to pull Gideon out, and Gideon choosing to go in, because the debt was always his to inherit.

chapters.title: Sealed from the Inside
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, final entry. He shuts the door from within and writes the last page of his record by the amber light: the account settled, the name returned, the Crane ledger closed. The last line: 'If you're reading this, the door is shut, and I am the seal.' Emotional beat: sacrifice as the final act of documentation — a prayer completed.

chapters.title: The Reading of the Record
chapters.summary: Ezra's POV. Recovering, Ezra buries his brother's notebook at the head of an empty grave and reads the entire record aloud at the funeral — the crime, the name Abigail Voss, the debt, the payment. Marge stands witness. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into testimony; the truth finally inherited instead of the debt.

chapters.title: The Last Winter
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Ezra's POV, one year later. The land is quiet; the excavation is filled; the house is cold in the ordinary way. But each first snow, Ezra finds a fresh page in his brother's notebook, in Gideon's handwriting, a single line: 'Still keeping the record.' He adds his own beneath it. Emotional beat: haunted peace — love outlasting the door, and winter as vigil rather than threat.
